composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
Reverently paying homage to the Triple Gem, this is the instruction for beginners according to their capacity, concerning the Dharmakāya of Sarvajña.

I pray that the Sage will take pity on me and grant his permission; this was composed during the summer retreat at Xingtang Monastery in Suizhou, and I have sent it to Lingyan Monastery on Mount Tai to be entrusted to Cishen for preservation and recitation.

Section on Receiving and Maintaining, Chapter Thirty-One: One. The Five-Character Explanation of the Dharma Title for the Method of Purifying the Mind through Contemplative Admonition. Section One: Regarding "Purifying the Mind," this refers to teaching you the cultivation of remedies for the various faults and afflictions currently active within you, so that you may attain liberation accordingly at once.

As defilements gradually subside, the mind becomes increasingly bright and pure; concentration and wisdom arise, and one gives rise to pure Mahāyāna faith, proceeding toward the dwelling place of the bodhi-lineage.

Because a subtle cause now will result in a corresponding fruit later, I therefore instruct you to examine the illness and apply its remedy, to promote meritorious deeds, to cultivate entry into the realm of faith, and to perfect the power of the roots of certainty.

As for the Three Sages and Ten Saints, the stainless and wondrous enlightenment, and the ultimate truth of the forty-two stages of the school of emptiness, one can only know and hear their coarse manifestations as images; these are beyond the reach of the power of ordinary beings of the lower stages, and they are likewise unable to practice them.
Now, I shall only cause you to purify and remove the adventitious dust and cataracts from the mirror of karma, so that you may perceive a small portion of the Buddha-nature within your own body.

You should drink the nectar of Prajñā and wash away the veils and entanglements, gradually manifesting the pure mind; if the mind is pure, it will purify the realm of sentient beings, and once sentient beings are purified, the Buddha-land is purified.

First, one eliminates afflictions to make the precepts pure; once the precepts are fully perfected, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes pure in turn. Through the purity of precepts and concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is made pure; once wisdom is purified, the source of one's own body is revealed. Because this principle exists, it is called "purifying the mind."
In the following chapters, although the methods for treating faults differ, they are all collectively termed "Purifying the Mind.

"Admonition" (誡) means to cause you to recognize the primary gateway of counteractive measures: first, eliminate coarse defilements and fundamental evil karma; then, by understanding the illness and its medicine, guard the mind and be cautious with speech; and finally, exert yourself in cultivating the Way to depart from faults and afflictions—therefore, it is called "Admonition."

"Contemplation" means examining the meaning; it involves observing whether this precept accords with or does not accord with the Buddha-dharma, as well as its obstacles and faults, and scrutinizing its names, phrases, and verses with careful reflection until one attains a realization of reality and grasps the original intent of the precept.

Furthermore, it can accord with the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā; as these two dharmas are the beginning of concentration and the source of wisdom, they give rise to and develop all factors of dhyāna and the limbs of the path, and are therefore called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).

"Dharma" refers to this very text of admonitions, arranged in its initial sequence, which is earnestly and clearly revealed with the intent to cause the prohibition and severance of afflictions, the cessation of all evil karma, and the application of superior progress so as to abide in a non-retrogressive mind; therefore, it is called "Dharma."
The five points of this method for contemplating the admonition on the pure mind are present throughout all the following chapters; they must be understood. 2.

Preface to the Admonition on Contemplation: The Fundamental Dharma of the Admonition on Contemplation. Second: Now, those who wish to cultivate the Way must first sever the two attachments of wealth and sensual desire among the three karmas.
If one does not crave wealth, there will be no flattery or contention; if one does not crave form, there will be no feverish affliction.
As the Sūtra says:
"Renouncing and turning away from desire accords with the factors of enlightenment."

"One should cultivate the contemplation of the body, exerting oneself with single-minded diligence to eliminate worldly craving and attachment; subduing defilements and afflictions to purify the mind; severing the pursuit of wealth and sensual pleasure to establish untainted roots of goodness; perfuming the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to form seeds of non-attachment; and gradually exhausting all delusions and taints to enter the stage of the noble ones."

Now, those who profess to understand the Dharma still greedily crave wealth and sensual pleasures, thereby nourishing their fetters and afflictions; being bound by these outflows and entangled by evil karma, they fall into the three miserable realms.

The Sūtra says: "Being neither a seeker of the Way nor a layperson, they have no name. Because they seek profit excessively, they devote themselves exclusively to lip-service and the cultivation of flowery, ornate rhetoric;

they engage in frivolous debate and contention, slandering and envying one another. Their three poisons grow ever stronger and their afflictions increase, causing them to sink into the sea of suffering. Knowing what they ought not to do, they commit offenses intentionally; thus, there will be no time of liberation, and even when a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, they shall neither see nor hear them.

Due to these causes and conditions, having completed his punishment in hell, he received the body of an evil dragon as a result of stealing the Buddha’s robes and food, and the defilements of broken precepts and anger.
As stated in the *Andha-nāga-sūtra*:
"Though one may understand and interpret the meaning [of the teachings], one cannot escape the suffering of one's karma."

"You should rely upon these admonitions and practice according to what has been taught. Accord with the specific remedy for each illness and attain liberation accordingly; purity cannot be attained through mere words.

Among the three poisons and five fetters, whichever is most predominant should be treated first; when the heavy ones are cured, the light ones will naturally subside. Don the armor of precepts and meditative concentration to destroy the demonic thieves within the mind."
The causes and effects of all suffering have wealth and sensual desire as their root;
the causes and effects of all happiness have precepts and meditative concentration as their root.

Yet these causes and effects all reside within the minute particles of the minds of sentient beings; for what reason do you not first restrain other transgressions, but instead issue a warning against wealth and sensual desire?
A Mahāyāna sūtra states:
"The eighty-four thousand karmic offenses that obstruct the Path all have wealth and sensual desire as their root. Why is this so?

Since beginningless time, sentient beings of the ten directions have killed one another for the sake of wealth more times than the number of motes of dust, and those who have killed for the sake of form exceed even that number.

For the sake of wealth and form, both the monastic and lay classes now undergo thousands of kinds of suffering within the one hundred and twenty-six great hells; only after passing through immeasurable kalpas do they enter the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
Whether monastic or lay, both are equally harmed by wealth and sensual desire; though they may initially uphold the precepts, they later transgress them, and those who can avoid this are rare.
If there are those who sever [these attachments], they are called practitioners of the Bodhisattva path, true upholders of the precepts, worthy sages, and disciples of the Buddha.

Although the two matters of wealth and sensual pleasure appear superficially trivial, the retribution for the offenses they provoke is exceedingly grave. Deceptions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise from wealth and sensual pleasure; these two faults can destroy the bonds between sovereign and minister, teacher and disciple, and husband and wife, and they likewise ruin internal and external kin, friends, and spiritual associates.

If one were free from wealth and sensual desire, there would be no further world; humans and devas would be liberated from suffering, praised alike by the noble and the ordinary, and with all outflows extinguished, they would advance to the fruit of Buddhahood. For this reason, wealth and sensual desire are the two things for which one must first issue a warning.
Arrogance arises from physical beauty, and stinginess arises from wealth; when one is both arrogant and stingy, even if they possess other virtues, these are not worth regarding.
First, sever attachment to wealth and beauty so that your meritorious practice may be established; afterwards, listen to the sutras and śāstras—this is the sequential order for entering the Way.
Because it proceeds swiftly against the current, it is called the "Pure Mind. The verse says:
Afflictions are like the sands of the Ganges; First, sever the two kinds of evil:
The first is wealth, the second is form; At the time of death, the spirit shall have no fear.
One should guard against even minor transgressions (*duṣkṛta*), let alone committing the four grave offenses.
With the three clusters of precepts (*triskandhaka*) pure, one rejoices at heart during the *poṣadha*.
You base person who craves wealth and beauty, I admonish you: sever your greedy attachments!
Wealth brings suffering throughout the three periods of time; because of form, one enters the fiery cauldron.
Form can obstruct the Noble Path, and wealth can cause conduct to become thin.
Examine your own mind with careful scrutiny; know that craving is madness and delusion.
The wise avoid [evil] as if it were a pit of fire; the stubborn and foolish do not find it loathsome.
If one commits an offense, one should repent and eliminate it; once eliminated, do not commit it again.
All things that possess form will ultimately end up filling the ditches and ravines.
By maintaining the precepts and restraining the mind from suffering, one will later receive great peace and happiness.

Chapter Three: The Method of Contemplation for the Five Stopping-Mind Meditations (Pañca-vinodana-samādhi). Regarding the five delusions: just as one removes a thorny tree by first cutting its roots, so too does one cultivate the five stopping-mind meditations to extinguish the five faults, halting them so they do not arise; therefore, it is called "stopping-mind meditation" (*vinodana*).
By practicing this contemplation, present afflictions cease to arise, and one attains "minor liberation.
Wherever one proceeds, through the discipline and pliancy of precepts and meditative concentration, one gradually realizes supernormal powers; this is called "great liberation.
When the ten obstacles are completely extinguished, it is called "true liberation."

None of these fail to rely upon the five methods of cessation and contemplation (*pañca-viṣkambhaṇa-dharma*) of the present; practicing and entering [the path] in this manner is called "purifying the mind.
The verse says:
Knowing for oneself that desire and passion are abundant, One should single-mindedly contemplate impurity.
Through renunciation one attains liberation; when desire is exhausted, one immediately gains concentration.
If one pursues discursive debate, the thought of desire will instead blaze more fiercely;
this is not the true remedy, but a downward path leading into a perilous track.
Knowing oneself to be full of anger, one should cultivate loving-kindness and compassion exclusively;
thus the fire of poison becomes cool, and one achieves the excellent discipline (*śīla*).
If one pursues mere scholastic debate, it will not be a remedy but only wearying toil.
Greed and hatred increase further, and one is heavily shrouded by the net of afflictions.
Realizing for oneself that delusion is great, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination;
only then does one awaken to the suffering of saṃsāra and come to understand the non-existence of self and person.
If one pursues discursive debate, one will see contention and clamor all day long;
seeking the branches and leaves while abandoning the root, one cannot uproot the source.
Knowing for oneself that self-conceit is great, one should contemplate the eighteen elements with precision.
Only when one realizes there is no person to be found can the sickness of the "self" be cured;
if one pursues debate and discussion instead, it will only increase one's debts in the three miserable realms.
Calculating for oneself and constantly seeking victory, fame and profit become one's own shackles.
Knowing that my distracted thoughts are many, I constantly count my inhalations and exhalations;
as mindfulness and discernment gradually take form, may they augment my power of precepts and meditative concentration.
If I were to pursue discursive debate, the clamor and dust of the world could not be stilled.
"Alternately asserting and denying one another—when will the consciousness of phenomena be extinguished?
This refers to the seven preparatory stages (*saptaprayoga*) within the Abhidharma:

the five contemplations for cessation (*pañcanivaraṇa-vipaśyanā*) are called the first preparatory stage; the remaining distinct-characteristics mindfulness-establishment (*viśeṣalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), general-characteristics mindfulness-establishment (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*), the stage of summits (*mūrdhan*), the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), and the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) are called the seven preparatory stages.

By accomplishing this contemplative practice, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*. Whether entering the path for the first time, practitioners of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna universally cultivate this contemplation.
The verse says:
"For what reason are the five cessations taught, And why are they not explained according to the scriptures?"
Preaching medicinal prescriptions while harboring illness is done solely for the sake of fame;
ordinary people crave gain and offerings, lacking the intent to cure their own deluded passions.
If one cultivates the five contemplations for cessation, one will certainly achieve success in the path of cultivation.
For what reason should one cultivate the five methods of stabilizing meditation (pañca-vastu-pratipakṣa) instead of pursuing discursive study?
There are two essential factors:
first, the sequential entry into the path according to the Buddha’s teachings, which serves as an antidote to coarse and heavy afflictions (dausthulya-kleśa).

Second, those who see and understand the meaning of the Dharma, yet knowingly and intentionally transgress it; they do not fear the Buddha’s precepts and do not cultivate dignified deportment, completely breaking all the pure precepts of the five categories.
Seeing others uphold the precepts, they instead give rise to hatred and slander; they crave only wealth and sensual pleasures.

Driven by anger and affliction, they engage in strife, and being stingy, envious, and arrogant, they lack both shame and remorse. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they will inevitably fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, remaining there for many kalpas.

One should contemplate this matter and verify it through direct experience; therefore, by practicing the five cessations (pañca-nivāraṇa) to stifle faults and give rise to the Path, one accords with the Buddha's teaching, and this is called "purifying the mind."
The verse says:
Greed has the nature of a jackal or wolf; hatred has the mind of a malevolent dragon.
Because they destroy the Dharma, they violate the prohibitions; they defile the precepts and commit lewdness.
Seeking to eliminate poison through the perception of dharmas, one instead commits even deeper transgressions;
creating karma with a heart free of remorse, at the end of life one approaches the Forest of Blades.
Falling into the Great Avīci Hell, the Buddha-nature sinks for kalpas on end.
Just as one whose official post has been revoked is punished and, having lost their influence, is unfit for office,
how can those who break the precepts consume the food of the people with such arrogance and self-indulgence?
What is the hand that breaks the precepts?
It is receiving the gifts of others' wealth and property.
What is the body that breaks the precepts?
Reclining and sitting upon fine beds and cushions;
what kind of unwholesome conduct is this?
Accepting the prostrations of others as sufficient for oneself.
What is the practice of breaking the precepts?
It is to silently accept praise and acclaim.
If one commits these five transgressions, all the devas will together lament with sorrow.
In Buddhism, those who have newly received the precepts study the Vinaya for five years before studying the Sūtras.
There are five divisions of the Vinaya:
first, the *Dharmaguptaka*; second, the *Mahīśāsaka*; third, the *Sarvāstivāda*; fourth, the *Mahāsāṃghika*; and fifth, the *Vimukti*.

These five schools of Vinaya constitute a single great canon of discipline (*vinaya-piṭaka*), the textual expressions of which are so vast and extensive that they are difficult to fully comprehend at once.

Now, those who wish to understand them should take wealth and sensual desire as their primary focus; if one can sever attachment to wealth and sensual desire, this is precisely what is called "upholding the Vinaya."

Through the purity of the prohibitions and precepts, one gives rise to meditative concentration and wisdom, accomplishes the Noble Path, and understands the essential framework of the Vinaya; for this reason, it is called "purifying the mind.
The verse says:
Within the five divisions of the Vinaya, the core principle is the severing of wealth and sensual desire.
Practicing the meditation on impurity, he countered his own self-indulgence with restraint.
Sighing over corpses in the forests and wilds, his inner heart was filled with compassion;
realizing that his own body would likewise inevitably become so, the fever of his craving was instantly extinguished.
The three poisons are exceedingly powerful; subdue them with the power of wisdom.
For clothing, seek out tattered and worn garments; for food, eat but one sitting.
Always practice an impartial mind; keep the intention pure and ever upright.
If one cannot act in this way, the *kāṣāya* will merely cover thorns.

The holy teachings have ten thousand variations because the dispositions of sentient beings differ; as the remedies for their ailments are manifold, the ignorant become confused. Though they expend great effort, it is not the correct antidote; they greedily crave fame and profit, thereby increasing their defilements all the more. Therefore, one should first cultivate the five *sthāpanā*s and subsequently study the expositions and discussions. To know this sequence is called "purifying the mind."
The verse says:
People of the world practice much learning, yet have never put even a fraction of it into practice;
with deluded minds they grasp at delusive dharmas, giving rise to strife and turmoil.
Entering the Way follows a sequential order; precepts and meditative concentration provide self-cultivation. Maintain a pure livelihood like that of Kāśyapa; do not be like the group of six. 4.

The Fourth Method for Admonishing and Contemplating the Measurement of Mental Conduct within the Final Dharma. Ordinary people understand the meaning [of the teachings] entirely through listening and study, thereby becoming knowers of the Dharma. Yet they may commit the four grave offenses, possess the eight kinds of impure wealth, and consume worldly delicacies, being without shame or remorse. They knowingly and intentionally transgress while having no fear of future retribution. For this reason, I cause you to measure your own mental conduct: first purify the prohibitive precepts, and only thereafter listen to the sutras. By employing these five admonitions, you shall be called one who has attained a pure mind.

In ancient times, those of great virtue lectured on a single fascicle commentary for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Later, Dharma Masters produced a three-fascicle commentary. In the present age, lecturers have produced ten-fascicle commentaries for the single chapter "The Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmi*); each vies to display their own capabilities and competes to manifest flowery rhetoric, yet the texts are so vast and extensive that there is nowhere for the mind to rest.
However, since the text is essentially identical to its meaning, why rely on human speech?
The foolish people of today seek only the names and not the Dharma; yet even the Dharma should not be clung to, let alone the written words, for the Dharma transcends words and language is cut off.
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states:
"The scriptural text is one and the same, yet the preachers offer divergent interpretations.
Each person relies on their own views to corrupt and disorder the True Dharma; because the celestial deities become incensed, the three calamities arise simultaneously.
For this reason, the Buddha-dharma has become insipid, like a single *sheng* of curd diluted with ten *hu* of water; it may appear to have the color of curd, yet when eaten, it lacks flavor.
Reflect carefully upon these discourses: human sentiment attempts to fathom the Buddha, but how could a person ever fathom the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom?
To investigate in this manner is called "purifying the mind.
The verse says:
The teacher who expounds the Dharma Ascends the high seat in two ways.
First, immeasurable merit; second, freedom from faults.
For one who has accomplished a mind of loving-kindness, the gift of Dharma surpasses material wealth.
Hatred and defilement do not belong to others; they are like sitting or lying upon thorns.
With outflows as the foundation and ignorance as the root,
if one interprets the sutras without removing these poisons, the Dharma Master will bring harm upon himself.
With a thieving mind seeking fame and profit, he acts in haste without reflection.
When an infant wishes to climb a ladder, he must first ensure his feet are firmly planted.
A scholar who is clever, yet whose movements are often frivolous and impulsive,
may misunderstand the meaning of the teachings, falling into wrong views and perversions.
Therefore, concentration remedies agitation; among the seven factors of enlightenment, this is the essential dharma.
By practicing concentration and wisdom in equal measure, the knowledge of all modes becomes subtle and wondrous.
While the World-Honored One was in the world, he taught only the cultivation of renunciation.
Cultivate goodness without becoming complacent; avoid even small evils from afar.
Moment by moment, contemplate impermanence; diligently practice the true antidotes.
With tranquil mind, study *dhyāna*; what need is there to cling to written words?
For what reason did all those who, while the World-Honored One was in the world, attained the Noble Path or were reborn in the heavens,
study according to the sequence and not transgress the Vinaya, entering the Way through proper means?

For five years he practiced the precepts; by night he cultivated meditative concentration to collect the mind and maintain its focus on the object, dwelling peacefully in forests and wilds without storing food beyond his needs. Possessing few desires and a sense of shame, he single-mindedly contemplated impermanence and impurity, remaining free from frivolity and with a mind undistracted.

In all your movements and comings and goings, always maintain purity and cleanliness; avoid unseemly appearances, and take the initiative to offer greetings. Through these wholesome conditions, you shall all attain the traces of the Path.
If you can single-mindedly study according to this, it is called "purifying the mind."
The verse says:
When realizing the Path of the True Dharma, one purifies the dharmas and disciplines sentient beings;
according to the specific matter, one performs the *karmavācanā*, thereby removing defilements and attaining the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
When the Semblance Dharma reaches its end, the *karmavācanā* rites will fall into disuse;
though they may appear to be in harmony, assemblies will give rise to strife.
All the various sūtras and vinayas are like ambrosia, yet they are also like poison.
Though one may understand the teachings, a hundred ailments remain unhealed; though one does not eliminate them, the disease breaks out again.
If one knows the Dharma but does not direct it toward the mind, understanding of the sutras will grow increasingly thin.
Abandoning the practices of precept and concentration, one gives rise to attachment toward mere words and letters.
Therefore, these verses were composed in rhythmic meter; when recited, they bring joy to the heart.
Sitting in stillness, one should contemplate them well, observing and reflecting upon them for oneself.
For what reason were these verses of repeated praise composed?
The words are few, but their meaning is vast and broad.
Rely on the precepts to benefit your person; accept them with faith and do not harbor doubts or aversion.
Even if you see others reviling or slandering you, remain indifferent with a mind free from contempt.
This is according to the Mahāyāna teachings, which do not contradict the principle. **Chapter Five:

Admonishing Contemplation of the Six Difficulties and Self-Rejoicing for Cultivating the Path.** First, among the myriad classes of beings, a human body is difficult to obtain. As the *Tiewei jing* (Sūtra of Trapuṣa and Bhallika) says:
"Now that one has obtained a human body, it is more difficult [to encounter] than a turtle [hitting] a wooden [stump]."

Second, although one may obtain a human body and be born in a central land, this very land shall be situated within a border region, yet it will be fully endowed with the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya of the True Dharma.
Third, although the True Dharma exists, it is difficult to have faith and delight in it; now, I follow my capacity to believe and dare not harbor doubt or slander.
Fourth, a human body is difficult to obtain; now, having received this male form with no physical defects, my features are fully perfected.

Fifth, although one possesses a male form and lacks no deficiency in the six sense faculties, it is extremely difficult to leave the household life when entangled and defiled by the five desires; yet now, having been able to sever these attachments to leave home and cultivate the Way, you have donned the robes of the Buddha and received the pure precepts of the Buddha.

Sixth, although you have received the prohibitive precepts, it is extremely difficult to follow them; therefore, you should respect and delight in the Vinaya, maintaining a sense of shame and dread of blame while guarding them with care.
If one does not contemplate these six matters, one will immediately fall into negligence, which deeply obstructs the Noble Path.

Having transcended the six difficulties, one should always rejoice; having attained what is difficult to attain, one must ensure that it is not lost. To reflect in this manner is called the pure mind.
The verse says:

There are six kinds of difficulties in the world; having already obtained what is difficult to obtain, one should diligently cultivate morality, concentration, and wisdom, and skillfully understand names, phrases, and sentences.
Therefore, those who study the Mahāyāna should know the proper course when questioned.
Having accepted food from a donor, if one fills the belly but lacks wisdom and reflection, then lacking wisdom, greed and anger will increase;
such a person cannot abide in accordance with the Dharma.
Violating prohibitions and destroying the precepts, one will be reborn in the four realms of existence at the end of life.

6. Precept on Contemplating Worldly Phenomena as Like a Dream and Cultivating World-Transcending Roots of Goodness. What skillful means can cause sentient beings to leave suffering behind and transcend the world?
Only the foolish crave and love; I, however, do not crave. What is it that is called the worldly fool’s craving? It refers to official rank and honors, carriages, horses, and treasuries;

towers, pavilions, gardens, and groves; maidens, music, fine garments, and delicacies; games, hunting, banquets, and performers; marriages and social gatherings; reliance on one's clan and lineage; pursuing friends and seeking influence; the arraying of the three armies, vanguard units of elite troops, strategic counsel and military tactics, boldness and slaughter, the pacification and eradication of enemies; the gratification of desires and the pursuit of pleasure; the siege of cities and the breaking of stockades; the binding of captives and the collection of taxes; the wielding of pen and brush by the heroic and chivalrous; the establishment of ambitions, secular arts, medical prescriptions, craftsmanship, accumulation of wealth, and the performance of ancestral sacrifices and offerings.

To speak briefly, regarding these numerous worldly affairs—immeasurable acts of killing, drinking alcohol and eating meat, disputes over victory and defeat, enmity and affliction, sorrow and joy, safety and peril, and good or bad fortune, calamity or blessing—one who is able to completely renounce and depart from them all is called a true practitioner of the Way, a person who has transcended the world.

Sentient beings are deluded and inverted; regarding these worldly matters as the true Dharma, they do not know that for countless kalpas they have endured the great suffering of birth and death, and that upon the destruction of the body and the end of life, they fall into the three evil realms, where they undergo intense burning and boiling for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Although they encounter such suffering, they still harbor greedy attachments to birth and death without weariness, mutually perpetuating their delusions regarding sensory objects; all this is due to not having encountered a virtuous guide and not having heard the True Dharma.
Now that you have heard this, to practice and train according to what you have heard is called "purifying the mind.
The verse says:
The nature of ordinary people is wild and deluded; what they perceive is always incorrect.
Nourishing the body of the three poisons, greed and hatred increase ever more intensely.
Without observing the impure form of a corpse, one carries away filth as if walking through a secluded place;
constantly wandering through environments of favor and opposition, one gives rise to deceit, hypocrisy, flattery, and sycophancy.
In reality there is no permanence, self, bliss, or purity;
yet through deluded views of permanence, self, and purity, one wanders forever upon perilous paths due to the inversion of sinful karma.
The wise understand according to reality; their life of wisdom and mind are resolute.
Contemplating the world as like a dream or an illusion, one exhausts the true Way and becomes a sage. 7.
Admonition on Contemplating Monks and Nuns Who Break the Precepts and Do Not Cultivate the World-Transcending Dharma.
Seventh: Those monks and nuns who break the precepts are those who keep male and female slaves and servants.
Oxen, donkeys, vehicles, fields and houses, plantations, groves, flowers and fruits; gold, silver, grain, and white silk;
screens, felt rugs, and blankets; fine pillows and delicate mats; chests, caskets, basins, and jars; bronze vessels, platters, and bowls;
excellent sets of the three robes; ivory beds and cushions; rooms, sheds, and outbuildings; kitchens, storehouses, water-mills, and oil-presses; and lard.
He enjoyed various flavors such as noodles, medicinal wines, and diverse sauces and vinegars;

he was highly regarded by princes and nobles, possessed the karmic conditions for wealth and status, and frequently visited relatives and old friends. He sent gifts, offered condolences, and submitted petitions to government offices.
As a leader among the masses, his disciples were numerous and influential, and he delighted in music while engaging in debates and discussions on the teachings.
He constantly resided in a single monastery to deliberate on monastic affairs and mutually impose censures and punishments.
He inquired about matters such as droughts and floods, abundance and scarcity, bandits and thieves, fire and water, and venomous beasts.
He passed by wine shops, market stalls, butcher shops, and hunters' dwellings, and [encountered] relatives, women, lutes and harps, and poetry.
Regarding such things as the composition of rhapsodies, playing go and double-six, reading heterodox scriptures, engaging in lofty discourse and loud laughter,
harboring resentment and engaging in disputes, drinking wine and eating meat, wearing garments of fine silk in the five brilliant colors,
diligently shaving one's beard and hair until the nails are as sharp as blades, and possessing the eight impure things with abundant wealth and treasures— within these matters...
To be greedily attached to worldly affairs, to amass possessions without relinquishing them, is called true breaking of the precepts.

A sutra states: "Such bhikṣus are called shaven householders; they are called thieves wearing the kāṣāya; they are called shaven hunters; they are called those of the three evil realms; they are called shameless people; they are called icchantikas; they are called slanderers of the Triple Gem; they are called those who destroy the eyes of all donors; they are called seeds of birth and death; and they are called obstacles to the Noble Path."
"To remain far removed from these ten kinds of evil is what constitutes a pure mind.
A verse says:
"How strange are ordinary people, who accumulate greed, hatred, and delusion!"
Violating the precepts without shame, they treat the treasure of the *vinaya* with contempt.
They pursue their aims with a frantic haste like fire;
though they plant seeds with great toil and hardship, when they instruct others to give much in alms, they themselves would rather have their sinews torn out.
Arrogant spiritual friends, relying on this body of pus and blood, Indulging in negligence and attached to the five desires— When will you emerge from the mire of suffering?
In clothing, you crave garments of five colors; In food, you crave constant fullness of the belly.
Having abandoned tranquility to enter the clamor of the world, he has never beheld the sutras or the precepts.
He pulls weeds and digs the earth, irrigating and tending his garden;
his worldly livelihood exceeds that of a commoner, yet he dwells with only three or five jars.
Anxious only that their wealth be insufficient, they bolt their doors and lock their gates securely;
they laugh with loud voices and boastful words, for their flattery and arrogance have not yet reached all.
They violate the four grave prohibitions, charging forward as fiercely as tigers.
When the body perishes, one sinks forever into the depths; only after the retribution for sins is exhausted is one born among the barbarians.
One should reflect on how sentient beings are mad: shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, they lack the light of wisdom;
they crave only immediate profit and fail to see the calamities of the future.
Having left the household life in hope for tranquility and joy, one instead becomes busily pursued by worldly affairs;
clutching wealth, one suddenly meets the end of life, and the religious and the secular are ultimately parted.
One's evil nature is like a snake or a scorpion; one's wicked greed is like a jackal or a wolf.
Shaving one's head without true virtue, A lofty appearance leads to self-injury.
Hiding transgressions while seeking fame, One does not fear the sores of gain and offerings;
But a layperson who cultivates precepts and gives charity Will be born in heaven when their life ends.
This śramaṇa is perversely stingy; he does not contemplate emptiness or impermanence.
Knowing only how to create evil karma, he meets every circumstance with a wall before him.
Having broken the precepts and violated the sūtras and vinaya, he conceals his faults out of shamelessness.
"I act" and "I receive"—to whom, then, would the three miserable realms be sent?
Although there is no self, person, or phenomena, good and evil do not perish;
thus, the suffering of the cycle through the three realms continues, and birth and death within the six destinies endure long.
Regarding these various evils and faults, Be prudent and reflect well;
May you sever the causes of their continuity, And hold the mind as firm as a vajra.
The water of meditative concentration washes away afflictions, While the city of ethical discipline provides self-protection.
Virtuous as the Brahmā Śaṅkhakuṇḍala, He is seen in the Western Quarter upon his departure. **Chapter 8:

Admonition on Observing External Dignity While Internally Arising the Dharma of Wrong Livelihood.** Regarding wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): it refers to purifying one’s dwelling place, adorning the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), arranging banners, flowers, and various ritual implements; frequently washing and shaving oneself; constantly wearing the *kāṣāya*; covering the shoulders with robes and wearing boots; maintaining a perfectly orderly deportment; walking slowly and straight forward; speaking in a low voice and gentle tones; or remaining silent with eyes closed and head bowed; keeping the robe and bowl close to the body, and adhering to the outward marks of the Vinaya.

Yet, within his heart he constantly seeks fame and profit, hoping for others to invite him and treat him with courtesy, respect, and honor; he advances in the precepts and leads others while forcibly acting as a master; dwelling among his disciples, he hopes for their reliance upon him; and even when explaining the Sūtras and Vinaya, he raises difficulties when questioned.

By nature, he was full of resentment and looked upon others with hateful eyes; when slighted or provoked, he would not accept their apologies. Whenever he spoke, he delighted in uttering piercing and sarcastic words. Seeing others gain profit, his jealousy burned like fire in his heart. Having never cleared away the defilements of the sensory realms or the impurities of the mind, even while sitting on his meditation mat, he gave rise to evil thoughts and perceptions, clinging to distracted and chaotic notions regarding worldly desires, which caused him to have nightmares at night and suffer the loss of seminal purity.

Defiled thoughts permeate the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), binding the seeds of evil karma; this defilement is able to obstruct purity, causing birth and death to never cease and saṃsāra to be boundless, as one undergoes all manner of suffering and affliction.

When the three karmas are impure and contrary to the Eightfold Noble Path, being white on the outside but black within and following the eight heterodox paths, this is called wrong livelihood that deceives both ordinary people and sages; observing in this way is termed "purifying the mind."
The verse says:
Reciting the Sūtra on Impermanence with the mouth, while the body harbors notions of permanence;
seeking gain and offerings from others—such a person has not yet opened their eyes to perceive the truth.
Regarding the three robes, he desires only those that are fine; he refuses to wear those that are tattered and worn.
His inner mind is exceedingly coarse and wild, yet his outward appearance seems truly refined.
He deceives the people of the world, causing the Great Compassionate One to shed tears.
The noble sages do not praise them, and the benevolent deities do not protect them.
Their karmic obstructions increase day and night, while their precepts and meditative concentration stagnate moment by moment.
Though they possess two eyes, they further suffer from a pair of cataracts.
9. The Ninth Discourse: A Warning Against Grasping at Signs, Reliance on Virtue, and Deceiving the Buddha. It says:
"What kind of bhikṣu is said to be deceiving the Buddha?"

If one says, "I cultivate loving-kindness and compassion while that person is full of anger," or "I am able to practice generosity while such-and-such a person is stingy and greedy," or "I am endowed with pure precepts while that person violates them," or "I am diligent and energetic while that person is indolent," or "I possess wisdom while that person is excessively foolish," or "I now delight in tranquility while they are defiled by the clamor of the world," or "I maintain dignified deportment while that person is frivolous and restless," or "I abide in accordance with the Dharma while they do not."

Some rely on secluding themselves in the mountains and abstaining from grain, wearing patched robes and eating but one meal a day, remaining constantly seated without lying down, or dwelling among tombs and beneath trees; others lecture on the sutras and vinaya, skillfully understanding the characteristics of dharmas, thinking, "I possess such merit and wisdom."
To grasp these marks is called the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span; to stubbornly cling to these marks is called deceiving the Buddha.
What is it that constitutes practicing the path so as not to deceive the Buddha?

If a person cultivates the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and yet does not give rise to attachment, they perceive only that conventional truth is false and inverted, like an illusion or a dream, without a single atom of reality.

Having accomplished this gate of contemplation, one cultivates morality, concentration, and wisdom; with diligence, one does not rely on one's own abilities to disparage others who lack virtue; being gentle, upright, humble, and free from contention, one dedicates these roots of goodness toward unexcelled bodhi. One who practices in this manner, detached from signs, is said to be one who does not deceive the Buddhas.

Because one does not deceive the Buddha, one attains the Dharma of equality; with the Dharma-eye clear and bright, one is able to purify the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and remains unattached to emptiness or existence—this is called the pure mind.
The verse says:
The eighty-four thousand dharmas Are remedies for manifold ailments.
This is called the great skillful means, accomplishing the practice of expedient mastery.
To grasp at signs is to deceive the Buddha; to cling to a self and give rise to views leads to contention.
Such bhikṣus sink into the depths themselves and cannot reach the ultimate goal.
Therefore, one cultivates the three gates of liberation;
with the emptiness of phenomena nourishing the life of wisdom, and through deep contemplation of dependent origination, one realizes knowledge with even greater joy.

10. The Teaching on Warning Against Arrogance and Fearing Others Regarding the Committing of Faults in Private Places. Ordinary people are haughty and deceitful, their deportment being inconsistent. To restrain oneself in the presence of others is called "deceit"; to commit faults in private places is called "arrogant negligence."

This refers to violating the precepts and decorum by drinking in private, stealing food, remaining naked and barefoot, bathing in rivers or ponds, voiding excrement in the open air, making sounds while passing wind, touching oneself in secluded places, sleeping on one's back or prostrating on the ground, squatting with the cheek resting on the hand, running about or looking around furtively, and chanting or whistling. To summarize, these are termed arrogance and flattery.

If one’s three types of action and four modes of conduct are entirely contrary to the Dharma—appearing human before others but like a ghost in private—all the celestial deities bear witness to this transgression. When the body perishes and life ends, one will be reborn among the macaques or among malevolent spirits; that the retribution for violating the rules of conduct arrives is precisely what is meant by "not deceiving oneself in a dark room."
Why is this? The tree of great karma possesses a radiance like a mirror, wherein all the karma created by sentient beings is fully revealed.
There are two kinds of divine spirits:
One character signifies being born together;
two characters signify sharing the same name.

Humans do not see Heaven, yet Heaven constantly sees humans. The power of karma sustains one’s transgressions regardless of day or night; thus, the practitioner must be cautious and maintain no distinction between private and public conduct.
The trichiliocosm resides within a single pore of the Buddha; how could it be that this is hidden away such that the worthy and holy ones remain unaware?

For this reason, Bodhisattvas possess eighty thousand modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), while Śrāvakas have three thousand. You should cultivate and assemble these modes of decorum, maintaining an equal application of mind whether in public or in private. Even at the cost of losing your life, you must not violate the model of benevolence. To maintain and practice in this manner is called "purifying the mind."
The verse says:
The noble ones have emerged from the three realms, yet they constantly traverse the domains of the three realms;
observing the karma of all sentient beings is like seeing reflections of forms against the sun.
The wise person is careful in their deportment;
Upholding the precepts with a courageous mind, they remain faultless even in private.
Firmly maintaining the four foundations of mindfulness, They contemplate the body as a venomous snake And examine the mind as an enemy.
Body and mind are a great affliction; They conceal transgressions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The wise, having committed an offense, repent; They never allow flaws or maladies to remain hidden.
Those who harbor their faults incur an evil reputation, And shall receive the iron fork in hell.
Alas, in this age of the final dharma, monks and nuns,
though their hair is shorn and their robes changed, still harbor greed, hatred, and delusion.
Pseudo-upāsakas and deceitful upāsikās— how lamentable!
In name they are called "observers of the five precepts," yet in reality not even one branch is complete.
Their mouths constantly recite medicinal prescriptions, yet they refuse to treat the disease of their own minds.
Because they are obscured by the veil of evil karma, they seek further sustenance through wrong livelihood.
The view of a self clings to the "I," yet it is not perceived as being separate;
nor does one observe the five aggregates, for the breath is like a suspended thread.
Before others, one restrains oneself with coarseness; in private, one exceeds Mount Sumeru.
I only fear the ridicule of men, yet I do not fear the witness of Heaven.
When lustful passions arise in drunken frenzy, my thoughts become defiled whether walking or sitting;
bound by these attachments, I break the heavy precepts and shall fall into Avīci at the end of my life.
One remains in hell for an eon; when the eon ends, one moves on again.
This suffering is difficult to endure; therefore, be most cautious in private.
Because they have created the karma of madness, all Buddhas give rise to great compassion.
The pleasure of committing sensual desire lasts but a moment, yet one suffers for immeasurable time.
A sutra says: From birth, a person possesses two kinds of deities;
day and night accompany the body, sharing its years.
In a single thought-moment, good and evil Are both clearly manifested before one.
When evil is great, days and years are diminished; When goodness is strong, life is extended.
The Buddha Vairocana’s Body and realm are vast and boundless.
Within a single pore, he accommodates three great thousandfold worlds;
his nature is luminously clear and penetrating, a supreme field of merit for all living beings.
Because the multitude possesses many faults, he gives rise to compassionate pity through no external cause.

11. The Eleventh Dharma-Instruction on Contemplating the Ten Evils of Women: As It Is, for the Sake of Disgust, Renunciation, and Liberation. Regarding the ten evils of women, a full exposition would be inexhaustible; therefore, I shall now speak of them briefly to inspire in you a sense of disgust and renunciation.
First, insatiable and immeasurable lust.
As the sutra says:
"In the lands of the ten directions, wherever there are women, there is hell."
"All obstacles to the Path constitute this suffering. When a woman desires a man, it is like the ocean swallowing rivers;

even throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, she is never ultimately satisfied. Obtaining one and gazing upon another, her mind becomes deranged; seeing a man who pleases her, she wishes to consort with him entirely. It is like fire receiving fuel—the more it is added, the more fiercely it blazes—so that whether walking or sitting by day or night, she never forgets the time for desire."

The bodies received throughout the five realms of existence are all comprised of female forms; since the beginningless past, the female organ has never been transformed, and even through the exhaustion of kalpas, one cannot escape the female body—therefore, it is called "insatiable greed."
Second, her envious heart is like a venomous serpent;

though she harbors loathing and defilement toward all those who resemble her own wife, her mouth feigns intimacy while her heart is that of an enemy, even as she conspires with her husband against others.

Whether by performing incantations or curses, administering poisons, hiring others to kill, severing limbs, disfiguring faces, depriving one of food and clothing, or by whipping and insulting—employing such means to eliminate others so as to stand alone—is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
Third is flattery and deceitful feigning of intimacy.
Whenever seeing someone, one smiles before speaking; though the mouth says, "I remember you," the heart harbors resentment.

In the presence of her husband, she thinks of other men, wishing for her husband to travel far away or wishing for his early death. She devises various schemes with outsiders, and when she sees her husband, she approaches him with flattery while her body faces him but her heart turns away—this is called feigning intimacy.
The fourth is negligence (*pramāda*).

It consists of thinking only of colorful garments, cosmetics, and hairpins or bracelets; grooming one's face and eyes in hopes of winning the affection of others; being addicted to the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) without distinguishing between kin and strangers; and having no fear of future lives as animals or hungry ghosts—this is called negligence.
Fifth is having much evil karma of speech. One’s words are false and deceptive, making it difficult to find sincerity;

whatever one discusses is mostly empty and rarely substantial. One delights in speaking vulgar, base, filthy, and evil words; mother and daughter, or sisters, do not avoid one another; one engages in double-tongued speech to sow discord and spreads rumors; one frequently makes oaths and vows without fearing karmic retribution; one slanders superiors in private and pursues litigation. This is called having much evil karma of speech.
Sixth, she shows aversion toward her husband.

Upon seeing a handsome man, she pursues him without shame, either by sending messengers to pressure him or by going there herself. She becomes restless while sitting or lying down, neglecting her domestic duties and livelihood. She may even fall ill or feign illness, eating and drinking in private while refusing to eat in public.

Her husband has acquired wealth through hardship and diligent labor, yet she squanders, steals, and diverts it to provide for her paramour; together they devise schemes intending to bring about his death.
Upon seeing her husband, she becomes enraged as if he were an enemy; this is called "disdaining and turning away from one's husband."
Seventh, most women harbor much guile and crookedness, making their true intentions difficult to discern.

For this reason, women are treacherous and their natures and capacities are hard to fathom; though they speak face-to-face, their minds remain a thousand li away, all because they greedily pursue worldly gain and their natures follow the superficial and frivolous.

They take what is right and cite it as wrong; they point to the void and turn it into reality. They constantly invert the natural order, finding many pretexts for every matter. Whether turning toward or away from something, whether affirming or denying its existence, their emotions follow the cold or the heat. Sometimes they rely on power and influence; sometimes they side with their kin and acquaintances. Sometimes they bring false accusations over wealth or beauty; sometimes they incite slander over the struggle for fame and status. Thus, their mouths are like greasy fat, while their hearts are like needles and knives.
Eighth is being greedy for wealth and disregarding kindness and righteousness. One’s parents raise and nurture them with arduous toil that is difficult to repay;

yet upon marrying and obtaining a husband, one abandons and forgets their benevolence and virtue. One schemed to divert the parents’ property to enrich the husband’s family, rejoicing when much is gained and resenting it when not. When the parents suffer from hunger and cold, one has no heart to provide for them; this is called being greedy for wealth and disregarding kindness and righteousness.
Ninth, the fire of desire burns the heart.

They feel no shame before their parents and have no fear of swords or staves; they may become pregnant while unmarried, run away to others, or entice others into their homes to commit transgressions, thereby bringing disgrace upon their parents and ruining their kin.

After being married, she again rebels against her husband; not long after her husband’s death, she thinks of marrying again; even when her sons and daughters have reached adulthood, she still abandons them to remarry. Her mind is deluded and intoxicated by desire, such that she avoids neither shame nor disgrace. The faults and afflictions of women are difficult to exhaust even throughout kalpas of time; therefore, it is said that the fire of desire burns the heart.
Tenth, the female body is foul-smelling, impure, and constantly discharging fluids.
During the heat of spring and summer, worms and blood flow out together. As the Sūtra says:

"Within the female organ there are twenty thousand lustful worms; their shape is like that of armlets, and they are as fine as the down of an autumn hair, reeking with a stench of raw flesh and filth."

I have suffered a miscarriage; my pregnancy and childbirth were filthy and chaotic, such that benevolent deities, upon seeing or hearing of it, all abandoned me, while malevolent ghosts and spirits came repeatedly to harass me.

"Such base and wretched things as these the foolish still crave; they abandon the foundations of mindfulness, break the pure precepts of the Buddha, and upon death enter the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts, suffering for long kalpas without any time of liberation."
These are called the ten kinds of evil karma of women; to be able to observe them and distance oneself from them is called "purifying the mind.
The verse says:
The four hundred and four kinds of diseases have undigested food as their root.
The sufferings of the three evil realms and the eight difficulties have woman as their root.
Birth and death throughout countless kalpas have craving as their root.
The bliss of liberation for the noble and holy ones has the renunciation of desire as their root.
The four snakes form the realm of the body; inverted perceptions constitute the mind.
Pus and blood fill the nine apertures, yet from thoughts of purity, lust arises.
What accords with one's desires is called happiness; those who lack faith fall into the Forest of Swords.
They receive retribution in the realms of pigs and dogs because their prior craving was deep.
The nature of all women is that truth is scarce while flattery and crookedness abound;
they do not contemplate the foul and impure body, but dwell upon desires while sitting and reclining.
Casting lustful glances at other men and taking pleasure in physical intimacy,
one will remain ultimately unsatisfied for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Having no shame before one’s parents, one brings ruin and destruction upon one’s kinsmen.
When there are more women than men in a household, the family declines and is repeatedly humiliated.
If a woman commits the ten evil karmas, after death she enters the Iron Bed Hell;
a great plowshare pierces her female organ, and she cries out in great agony and lamentation.
When the retribution for hellish sins has ended, one transmigrates into the womb of a sow;
devouring excrement and dwelling in latrines, one becomes a worm in foul filth within a privy,
again suffering the agony of being slaughtered and dismembered— thus the karmic retribution for accumulated eons finds no end.
Passing from the realm of animals into that of hungry ghosts, one’s foul food never suffices;
all limbs and joints burn with fire, yet the skeletal remains refuse to dissolve.
The pleasure of greed is but momentary, while the retribution one receives is endless suffering.

12. The Twelfth Instruction on Contemplating How the Four Requisites of a Donor Arise from the Conditions of Suffering: The instruction on contemplating how the four requisites of a donor arise from the conditions of suffering is as follows: the harming of life is called the karma of suffering, and the exhaustion of tendons and bones is called the condition of suffering.
The Sūtra says:

Regarding food, it involves plowing, sowing, weeding, reaping, harvesting, winnowing, storing in pits, transporting by cart, pounding and grinding, cooking on the hearth, steaming and boiling, briefly preparing, providing, and serving; furthermore, it includes planting vegetables, building walls, irrigating gardens and fields, and producing sauces and vinegars.

It is calculated that for one bowl of food, one bowl of sweat is produced; this sweat residing in the skin and flesh is none other than blood. Thus, the labor required for a single meal results in the production of one bowl of blood from the worker; how much more so when considering the many meals consumed throughout an entire lifetime?

From the initial plowing and sowing until the food enters the mouth, countless small creatures of various kinds are injured and killed; therefore, the Buddha’s precept is to take but one meal per day, sustaining life merely to pass through this single lifetime.

Regarding clothing: raising silkworms involves killing them in their cocoons; gathering mulberry leaves, weaving, threading, dyeing, washing, and tailoring require an immeasurable amount of labor and hardship through various conditions.

Calculating the resources for upper and lower garments, one must consider how many silkworms were killed and how much vital energy was expended, and how much suffering the silkworm cocoons endured when entering the boiling water. For this reason, the Buddha taught the wearing of *pāṃśukūla* (rag robes), so that by covering the coarse and humble physical form, one may hope to attain the cultivation of the Path.

Regarding dwellings: from the time walls are erected and pits are dug into the earth, one harms and kills the insects of the soil; when timber is felled, one harms and kills the insects of the forest trees; when bricks and tiles are made, one kills the insects in the clay and water; and when fire is set for smelting and forging, one kills the insects in the wood and grass.

Laborers expend their physical strength and donors waste their wealth; with food, drink, and various other conditions, the toil and loss are immense before even a single room is completed. Therefore, the practitioner finds peace by relying upon burial mounds, trees, and grass mats.

He reflects on food as suffering and eats while restraining the body; he reflects on clothing that takes life and wears robes of discarded rags; he reflects on dwellings and bedding as arising from conditions of suffering; he is devoted to the dhūta practices, moving only once every three months; and he reflects on the four requisites as difficult to digest, maintaining few desires and contentment.

The Sūtra says: "When receiving food from a donor, one should regard it as eating the flesh of one's own child during a time of famine; when receiving clothing from a patron, one should regard it as being wrapped in glowing iron; when entering a dwelling, one should regard it as entering an iron cauldron; and when using a bed or seat, one should regard it as a bed of glowing iron. It would be better to break this body into atoms than to receive the offerings of others with a body that has violated the precepts."

The bitter retributions of the three miserable realms all stem from attachment to clothing, greed for food, and the desire for fine dwellings. If one violates the precepts, one must repay the donor: either by becoming a slave or servant subjected to whipping and forced labor, or by assuming the form of a beast with fur and horns. While alive, one repays the debt through tendons and bones; at death, one returns it through skin and flesh. When the strength to bear burdens is exhausted, one rises only to fall again. The pleasure derived from receiving the faithful offerings of others is beyond description, yet the suffering endured while repaying the donor exceeds that pleasure ten thousandfold.
Therefore, I instruct you to know shame and dread of blame, and to carefully guard yourselves for future lives; do not break the precepts while receiving offerings—this is called a pure mind.
The verse says:
The wise do not crave food; Those who crave food lack wisdom.
One does not dwell on the hardship of expelling excrement, but takes only the benefit of human food.
One consumes the saliva within one’s own brain; what is gathered above is discarded below.
When the life-force of wisdom cuts off the four kinds of nutriment, the practitioner does not crave or relish them.
The bhikṣu finds no joy in tranquility; Greedily seeking profit, he accepts ritual requisites.
His mind is distracted by his pursuits, Hurriedly occupied with various affairs.
Having gained one thing, he looks for another; His mind schemes constantly, never remaining still.
One should feel shame before the donor, for this foul body is but a sack of rags.
I urge you to contemplate the three gates of liberation, to detach from signs and discipline yourself;
with few desires, learn contentment, and follow the example of the sons of Śākya.

13. The Thirteenth Precept on Contemplating the Endless Suffering of Rebirth and Retribution in the Flow of the Six Realms Sentient beings within the three realms have, since beginningless time, created good and evil karma. All of this perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), forming seeds of karma that are a mixture of pure and defiled, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Consequently, they undergo the retributions of the six realms, with birth and death being without limit.
Emerging from hell, they are born among the various devas, humans, ghosts, spirits, and animals.

Among the animals, they first take the form of crawling creatures such as scorpions and gadflies; in a single day and night, they die and are reborn a hundred times, dying and being reborn a thousand or ten thousand times before gradually attaining large bodies, even reaching those such as the makara fish, which are ten thousand yojanas long.
Having escaped from the body of an animal, one receives the body of an asura; when the merit of the heavens is exhausted, one is reborn again among the hell-beings and hungry ghosts.
As the Sūtra says:
"There are hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds of ghosts, each with its own distinct retribution."

The six classes of beings—humans and animals—each comprise thousands of millions of species; their physical forms, lifespans, experiences of suffering and joy, essential natures, appearances, and whether they are handsome or ugly differ in a thousand variations and myriad categories, such that it is difficult to exhaustively describe them all.
Now, regarding the fundamental karma and place of origin for those in the human realm, a sutra states:
"Those who receive a physical form with upright and handsome features, whose nature is pure and clean, have come from among the devas."
Those with coarse and unrefined skin who take no pleasure in practicing charity come from among animals;
those of ugly appearance, dull-witted, and lacking in intelligence come from the hells;
and those whose movements are fickle and restless come from among monkeys.
Those who are frivolous and flirtatious come from among the *kinnara* maidens;
those whose nature is full of flattery and sycophancy come from among the *yakṣa* spirits.
To speak briefly, it would be difficult to exhaustively describe them all at length.

Within a single realm of existence, there are causes and effects as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; one may undergo the body of a single ant for many kalpas, let alone when undergoing other forms or other realms. Therefore, birth and death are inexhaustible.

You should observe this closely: at the time of casting off body and life there is great suffering and pain; at the time of receiving a body and being born there is likewise great suffering and pain. Such suffering has already endured for aeons as numerous as motes of dust; you have already cast off countless bodies and have already undergone boundless suffering.

Fools still practice heedlessness therein; you should reflect upon this and strive diligently for deliverance, exerting yourself with single-minded application to achieve the fruit of no-more-learning and realize true liberation, which is blissful and secure.
One who can contemplate in this way is said to possess a pure mind.
The verse says:
All people in the world desire to experience happiness, yet they refuse to cultivate the causes of happiness.
The foolish person, upon obtaining pleasure, deems it eternal; unaware that at the end of life they shall be diminished.
At fifteen, their appearance and speech are lovely; by forty, they have become haggard and withered.
Even if one were born in heaven for eighty thousand kalpas, one cannot escape impermanence and will fall into the abyss.
Ordinary beings momentarily delight in pleasure while forgetting great suffering; when undergoing great suffering, they again forget their pleasure.
All such experienced suffering and pleasure are but empty flowers; fundamentally, they are nothing more than the errors of deluded sentiment.
When delusion is resolved and the Way is realized, one attains spiritual powers; forever severing birth and death is called true bliss.
14. The Fourteenth Discourse on the Teaching for the Great Wise One to Remain Unmoved by the Power of the Eight Winds. What are these eight?
First, gain; second, loss; third, defamation; fourth, praise; fifth, renown; sixth, insignificance; seventh, suffering; eighth, pleasure.
All sentient beings are moved by these eight and cannot find peace of mind for themselves; therefore, they are called the "Eight Winds."

What are the characteristics of movement? To gain profit one is immediately pleased; to suffer decline and affliction one is immediately distressed. To be insulted one becomes angry; to be praised one is delighted. Encountering suffering one harbors sorrow; meeting with pleasure one gives rise to indulgence. When commended, the heart rejoices; when subjected to sarcasm, one harbors resentment.

These eight dharmas cause ignorant worldlings to waver and remain in unrest; they treat praise and blame as one and same, giving rise to the two types of karma, creating the causes for the three miserable realms, and reaping the fruits of the four destinies. They surge through the five paths like waves, bringing about the ten fetters, remaining forever confined within the cage—when will they ever be liberated?

However, the ten realms arise through the harmony of conditions and cease because their nature is empty. When one realizes that arising and ceasing are thus, there is no resentment; the wind of resentment does not rise, the fire of sin does not burn, and the flames do not flare up. The mind attains cool serenity and is free from all feverish afflictions. Because it is free from such afflictions, it is called a "pure mind."
The verse says:
The fool craves delicious food, yet loathes the excrement within his belly;
he is passionately attached to life, yet treats old age, sickness, and death with contempt.
Censure and praise are like echoes; anger and joy arise alternately.
With a mind that grasps at signs, it fluctuates between high and low, failing to recognize the principle of equality.
Deluded by ignorance, they cling to sounds; such is the common way of ordinary beings.
Birth and death are like excrement and food; the scriptural texts distinguish between them.
Deceived by empty sounds, even immortals fall from cliffs to their deaths;
the wise understand the true emptiness, for seeing and hearing are not the same.

15. The Teaching on Contemplating the Characteristics of Body and Mind as Suffering, Affliction, and Calamity. Regarding the characteristics of the body (*kāya-lakṣaṇa*): it is a provisional formation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) belonging to the various classes of beings within the six realms of existence. It manifests as a present fruit in recompense for past causes; therefore, it is called the characteristic of the body.
The physical forms consist of eighty-four thousand types, with distinct differences between the primary and secondary retributions.
A single person has undergone such varieties of bodies throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; now, as you are cautioned to contemplate the body, it is limited only to the human realm.

A single person has ninety-nine thousand pores, through which eight hundred kinds of winds enter and exit; eighty thousand species of worms fill the entire body; four hundred and four diseases arise in alternation; three hundred and sixty joints support one another; one hundred and ten forms of suffering are never absent; and thirty-six kinds of impurities, pus, and blood combine to form this aggregate body, from which nine orifices leak foul fluids like festering sores. Thus, through such karmic suffering, a "person" is first formed. The noble ones abandon it as they would a loathsome disease; therefore, it is called "contemplating the body."

As for the characteristics of the mind: within a single thought-moment there are ninety kṣaṇas; arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing are like flashes of lightning. As sensory objects arise and consciousness is produced, one encounters greedy objects and invites retribution.
The Sūtra says:

"There are twenty-one thousand types of mind characterized by greed, twenty-one thousand types of mind characterized by anger, twenty-one thousand types of mind characterized by delusion, and twenty-one thousand types of mind characterized by equal proportions [of the three poisons]; together, these constitute the eighty-four thousand afflictions."
There are one hundred and eight kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*), five hundred and forty kinds of sensations (*vedanā*), and ninety-eight kinds of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Therefore, it is called "contemplating the mind.

If one enters the method of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) contemplation, the activities of the mind gradually subside, proceeding through the nine successive concentrations (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) until returning to the single, true, pure mind. This pure mind is called Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), the True and Eternal Dharma-body, the mind that is no-mind, and the mark that is no-mark. To contemplate in this manner is called "purifying the mind."
The verse says:
Abandoning conditions and relying on pure objects, sustaining the body through right livelihood,
contemplating the mind of emptiness with clarity, one attains liberation according to one's capacity.
If greed or anger should arise, one should observe emptiness to suppress them;
the roots of afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges can be severed by the power of meditative concentration.
To cultivate concentration alone without cultivating wisdom is the way of the Lesser Vehicle, not the Great Wisdom.
Though one may practice by mortifying the body, it is merely a waste of years;
only by cultivating concentration and wisdom in equal measure does one come to know the essence of Buddha-nature,
leading directly to Great Nirvana— how much more so for the truths of the mundane world!
*The Method of Contemplation for Admonishing the Mind and Purifying the Heart*, Volume Upper; *The Method of Contemplation for Admonishing the Mind and Purifying the Heart*, Volume Lower.

16. The Sixteenth Admonition on Contemplating the Pretense of Virtue to Spread One’s Fame: The Law of a Pure Mouth and a Turbid Heart. *The Admonition on Contemplating the Pretense of Virtue to Spread One’s Fame: The Law of a Pure Mouth and a Turbid Heart*, Number Sixteen.

The sages and worthies practice in secret; internally possessing wisdom, they appear foolish externally. Ordinary people, however, are mad and deluded; internally foolish, they appear wise externally.

They do not possess precepts or meditative concentration, yet they manifest the appearance of precepts and concentration; they proclaim their own good reputation to attract gain and offerings; they conceal their defilements and faults while outwardly displaying purity; and they constantly speak of their own merits to both monastics and laypeople.
The Sūtra says:
"This is a great thief without a sword; his sin exceeds that of plundering. Through deceit and fraud, he commits a grave offense and falls into the three evil realms.
A person who feigns virtue is fully possessed of five karmas:
First, the celestial deities do not protect him, bearing witness that he accepts offerings while deficient in the precepts.
Second, five thousand great ghosts constantly block his path ahead, shouting "Great Thief! and sweeping away his footprints.
Third, one may encounter great decline and affliction in the present life.
Fourth, one will never encounter a Buddha and will be born into a family of wrong views.
Fifth, one deceives oneself and deludes others; while one undergoes bitter retribution for oneself, the donor receives no fruit. These are the five karmas.
Therefore, I exhort you: attribute rectitude to others and draw the crookedness toward yourself; keep your virtues secret as hidden merit (*guṇa*), as if unable to speak of them.

Why is this? Goodness is like gold and jade—it does not require others to know it; evil is like filth and soil—it requires no concealment. The nature of filth and soil is that its value lies in being removed early, while fine goods and treasures are to be held firmly in silence.

The nature of contentment does not seek a good reputation; one who has few desires and dwells in tranquility need not fear an ill repute. Those who calculate in terms of a self desire fame and profit.
Yet, when one examines the body and finds no self, where can fame and profit abide?

When both fame and profit are empty, and when one is detached from the self, that is reality; by extinguishing both emptiness and reality, one correctly enters into equanimity. To be able to relinquish fame and profit is what constitutes a pure mind.
If you wish to attain a pure land, you must purify your mind; as your mind becomes pure, so too does the Buddha-land become pure—this is called "purifying the mind.
A verse says:
To leave the home life and practice what is contrary to the Dharma Brings about much suffering and affliction.
Perilous suffering follows in abundance, while true peace and joy are rare;
The devas do not protect them, and demonic activities repeatedly disturb them.
At the time of death they harbor fear, and for long kalpas they fall into the evil realms.
The profound and secret treasury of virtuous conduct is like a mani jewel;
all faults and evils are utterly extinguished, just as weeds are removed from the edge of a field.
In true practice one seeks no fame; precepts and concentration are clearly realized within.
Feigning virtue while concealing evil is not good within the Buddha-dharma.
Contemplate these admonitions with earnest attention and open heart;
regarding all causes that obstruct the Path, repent and never create them again.

17. The Seventeenth Teaching on Observing Sentient Beings Each Clinging to the Two Kinds of Retribution: the Primary and the Secondary. Sentient beings within the three realms dwell in firm attachment; because they crave these two kinds of retribution, they are obstructed from liberation.

The gods of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception consider their own attainment of *nirvāṇa* to be the ultimate fruit of retribution; harboring overweening pride (*adhimāna*), they do not realize that they have not escaped the three miserable realms.

The sentient beings of the Form Realm are greedily attached to the flavor of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-rasa*), considering their own bliss to be unsurpassed; furthermore, they take pride in the radiance of their bodies and the clarity of their palaces, thinking, "My fruit is the most excellent.

The sentient beings of the Desire Realm are by nature prone to negligence; craving the pleasures of the five desires, they fail to perceive impermanence, and when their heavenly merit is exhausted, they return once more to the evil paths.

Ordinary beings on the stage of thinness possess stinking bodies and inferior karmic retributions; giving rise to great arrogance, each relies upon their own views, claiming that among all people there is nothing superior to their own permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity.

The myriad species of animals, dwelling in nests or burrows, each cherish their own lives and do not aspire to the human or celestial realms; they do not loathe their own bodies nor do they seek the Pure Land.

This single body, though comprising various types of beings, universally experiences [suffering]; even down to venomous snakes and crawling insects, all cherish their lives and are greedily attached to their dwellings, yet they do not realize that within these bodies they equally possess Buddha-nature.
However, these various bodies have, since beginningless time, undergone transformation according to karma without a moment’s pause.

You should observe this closely and give rise to weary detachment; diligently seek skillful means to escape the dual retributions of the primary and secondary worlds of birth and death.
