If one relies upon a good person, there will be benefit day and night; yet if there is no skilled master, where can the mind be entrusted?
Since you have left the household life and received the Tathāgata’s precepts, should you lose your way even for a moment, you will suffer for long kalpas.

In this present age of the Final Dharma, the minds of sentient beings have become thin and impoverished; they turn their backs on gratitude and sever righteousness, easily becoming weary of their teachers and monks.
They delight in wandering and dwelling alone, seeking to satisfy their own whims and desires, yet they fear that by failing to act in accordance with the Dharma, they will fall into the evil realms.
Without lingering attachment or hesitation, I have composed these admonitions, briefly outlining and proclaiming the essential matters of human conduct.
As for other volumes, they are well known to all; as for the sutras and treatises of our own tradition, you should already possess them.
The essential meaning of the Mahāyāna is the same throughout the entire land; yet, were I to further reveal it, I fear the scrolls would become overly voluminous.

Simply washing your own mind is superior to a thousand verses. You should be like one who finds water when thirsty—drink as you please without gnashing your teeth—and read it in a quiet place; why trouble others with your view?
My subtle intention you have not yet understood; even though worldly people do not fully comprehend it, only those with the divine eye can bear witness to my mind.
"You should practice accordingly; you shall never be deceitful or mistaken.
Why do you seek in solitude and not allow others to observe you?
Only the sage associates with the sage; things are categorized by their kind. The foolish and the wise belong to different classes, and like gathers with like."

In the present age, scholars hold divergent views and constantly dispute one another, disparaging others while praising themselves; they laud their own positions and revile those of others, indulging in perverse sentiments, strange laughter, and idle chatter, all of which they vied with one another to commit to writing and preserve.
Their essential words are base and frivolous;
they desire broad knowledge but do not wish for broad practice;
they aspire to attain extensive understanding so as to stand out alone among the multitude.
They scheme to crave empty renown, seeking fame and reputation;
they turn their backs on body and mind, slyly stealing at profit and honor.
The three miserable realms are already at hand, and there will never be a time of escape.
The Sūtra says:

"Suppose one were to gouge out the eyes of a thousand people on a single day, and continued to gouge out many eyes in this manner day after day; the actual transgression committed by such a person would be heavier than that of the former."
To avoid such [criticism], you alone must take responsibility; it is not that there are many faults within these admonitions themselves.

In the world, there are difficult words, contradictory words, destructive words, flowery and ornate words, irrational words, repetitive words, foreign words, formal liturgical words, confusing words, agitating words, and bewildering words. Nowadays, later generations devote themselves exclusively to studying these types of speech. Those who understand them beforehand deceive those who do not; they merely practice frivolous debate—what has this to do with the cultivation of the Path?
The mouth is exhausted and the spirit weary, yet the mind receives not a single drop of nourishment; afflictions increase further, and the sense of self grows ever greater.

A lifetime of diligent toil results only in the squandering of merit and the absence of blessings; with the mind fixed on fame and profit, the pure heart is not examined. If one gains benefit through mere false names, by what means can it be digested?
It is like a great, fierce fire, difficult to endure and difficult to approach.

Furthermore, it is like speech that is in accordance with the Dharma, easy to understand, spoken from the body and mind, speech concerning the precepts, essential speech, speech free from fault, speech for curing obstacles on the path, speech that enters into principle, and speech of accomplishment. If one sees such speech as these, one claps hands and laughs loudly, unwilling even to look at it, let alone accept and uphold it.

You should seek [the meaning] slowly, contemplating each character; within a single character lies immeasurable meaning. If you read it directly, you will finish it in a short time, yet if you act according to these admonitions, you will not reach mastery in a lifetime.

The value lies in swift practice, not in rapid recitation; holding the text in hand and gazing upon it, one should shed tears, conceive the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find, as if seeing the World-Honored One himself.
Why is this? Because it proclaims and inspires others so that they may accord with the noble path;
it instructs you to purify your mind so that you may advance toward Bodhi.
In general, there are two kinds of meanings cautioned against in the sūtras and śāstras:
the first is that which accords with principle (*yoniśas*).

The secret treasury of the Tathāgata—the Dharma of emptiness and equality—eliminates appearances and enters into the ultimate; it is a profound, mysterious, and subtle realm unknown even to those in their final stage of rebirth (*kṣetragata*) and unfathomable to those of the Two Vehicles. This is called "accordance with principle."
Second, its phrasing and meaning are easy to understand and flow smoothly when read; or it may be composed in verse, beautiful and pleasing to the mind, which is called "conforming to the emotions.
Its characteristics appear as if shallow, yet through them one enters the profound; it discards all views as being correct and establishes all views as being false.
It is like the great ocean, where at first one enters until the water reaches the ankles, and as one gradually advances, there is no limit and the bottom cannot be found.
It is like a seven-day-old infant who has not yet digested rich food;
how could a common countryman ride in a palanquin?
To eat before having finished one's previous meal will surely result in choking;
to ride a carriage that is not strong enough is censured by the wise.
Yet the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma cannot be entered by those lacking wisdom; a jeweled terrace a thousand fathoms high cannot be ascended without a staircase.

When first entering the gateway of the Way, if one has not yet cultivated precepts and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*) but instead bypasses these to study the school of emptiness (*śūnyatā*),

the Buddha does not rejoice in it. Just as a base man who, having accumulated wealth over generations, should suddenly seize the state seal— the King would surely impose a severe punishment upon seeing him—
so too must one proceed from the five preliminary practices (*pañca-vastu-sthāpana*) to eliminate afflictions and realize the state of a sage.

This present admonition lacks elegance or artifice in its substance; out of deep compassion for you, I have pointed to specific matters with concise restraint. Furthermore, I regret that you have presumptuously occupied the position of my teacher’s head, remaining ignorant of my instructions.
Therefore, dispatch words that pierce to the core and enter the heart, as if speaking face-to-face, so that your practice of the Way may be perfected.
Once you have attained self-knowledge, in turn teach your fellow students and other wise ones.
I am extremely frail and my health has long been precarious; if I do not see you again, this shall serve as my final testament.
My words are not prolix, but they are intended to exhort you to purify your mind.
